meta.title: Business Continuity and Disaster Recovery Policy

blocks.content: Business Continuity and Disaster Recovery Policy
1. Purpose

This policy defines how the company prepares for, responds to, and recovers from events that disrupt its ability to deliver its core products and services — including regional cloud provider outages, data center loss, large-scale infrastructure failure, and events affecting critical vendors. It exists so that a disruption is met with a rehearsed plan rather than an improvised one, and so recovery time and recovery point commitments made to customers are backed by a tested capability rather than an assumption.

It also defines the company's obligations around annually testing its continuity plans, a control expected under ISO/IEC 27001:2022's business continuity domain and routinely requested by enterprise customers during security review.

A disruption large enough to trigger this policy is, by definition, rare, which is exactly why it must be governed by a written, rehearsed plan rather than improvised expertise: the engineers who best remember how a manual failover works are the ones who last exercised it, and without a mandated annual test that memory decays well before it is next needed for real.

This policy also exists because the cost of a Tier 1 outage is not linear with its duration: a ten-minute blip is an inconvenience customers barely notice, but the same outage stretched to four hours crosses into contractual service-level penalties, elevated churn risk, and in the most severe cases a public incident that draws regulator or press attention. The recovery time and recovery point targets in §4 are chosen specifically to keep the company on the right side of that threshold for its most critical systems.
2. Scope

This policy applies to every production system classified as Tier 1 or Tier 2 in the service criticality register, and to the teams that own them. Tier 1 systems are those whose unavailability directly stops customers from using the product; Tier 2 systems materially degrade the product but leave a usable, if limited, experience. Tier 3 internal tooling is out of scope for a full disaster recovery plan, though it must still have a documented restore-from-backup procedure.

The policy covers both technical recovery — restoring systems, data, and connectivity — and organizational continuity, such as maintaining customer communications and support coverage during an extended incident. It does not cover physical safety and evacuation procedures for office locations, which are governed separately by Facilities.

Organizational continuity also extends to the people who staff the response itself: the recovery plan for any Tier 1 system names at least two people capable of executing each critical step, not one, so that a disruption occurring while the primary owner is on leave, unreachable, or otherwise unavailable does not become a second, compounding failure on top of the original disruption.

The service criticality register itself is reviewed at least twice a year by Site Reliability Engineering together with each system's owning team, since a system's tier can change as the product evolves — a background batch job that was once Tier 3 can become Tier 1 the moment a customer-facing feature starts depending on its output in real time.

This policy assumes each Tier 1 or Tier 2 system already has a working backup and restore mechanism as a baseline capability owned by the system's own team under normal engineering practice; what this policy adds on top is the coordination layer — who declares an event, who authorizes a customer-visible failover, and how the response is tested and reviewed — not the underlying backup technology itself.
3. Roles & Responsibilities

Each Tier 1 or Tier 2 system has a named owning team responsible for authoring and testing its recovery plan, but the Incident Commander role coordinates the response the moment a disruption is declared, regardless of which team's system is affected.

The Incident Commander rotation is deliberately drawn from a pool broader than any single team, so that a disruption affecting the primary on-call engineer's own team does not leave the response without an independent coordinator. Serving in the rotation requires having completed the annual DR training and having participated in at least one live or tabletop exercise in the preceding twelve months; a rotation member who falls behind on either requirement is temporarily removed from the schedule until current.

blocks.content: 4. Procedure

A disruption moves through five stages: detection, plan activation, failover or workaround, recovery, and a post-incident review. Each Tier 1 system's recovery plan documents its specific recovery time objective (RTO) and recovery point objective (RPO); the default company-wide targets, absent a system-specific override, are a four-hour RTO and a fifteen-minute RPO for Tier 1 systems.

blocks.content: 4.1 Detection and Declaration

A disruption is typically first detected through the same monitoring and alerting that governs day-to-day incidents under the Incident Management and Response Policy (POL-005), §4. What distinguishes a disaster recovery event from a routine incident is scope and expected duration: if the on-call responder assesses that a Tier 1 system will be unavailable for longer than the incident policy's standard escalation window, or that its home region is affected rather than a single component, they escalate to the Incident Commander to consider formal DR activation.

The same escalation path applies when a Critical-tier vendor reports an incident under the Vendor and Third-Party Risk Management Policy (POL-008), §4, and that vendor supports a Tier 1 system. The Incident Commander evaluates whether the vendor's own recovery timeline is acceptable or whether the company should activate its own workaround.
4.2 Plan Activation and Failover

Once the Incident Commander declares a DR event, the owning team executes that system's documented recovery plan, which specifies the failover target (a secondary region, a standby replica, or a degraded-mode configuration), the steps to redirect traffic, and the verification checks to run before declaring the failover complete.

Customer-facing status communications during an active DR event are approved by the responsible Product Manager before publishing, to keep messaging accurate without disclosing operational detail that could complicate the response.
4.3 Recovery and Stand-Down

Recovery is considered complete once the affected system is verified against its RTO/RPO targets and normal traffic has been restored to the primary environment, or a decision has been made to remain on the failover target longer term. Only then does the Incident Commander stand down the DR event.
4.4 Post-Incident Review and Annual Testing

Every DR event, whether a real disruption or a scheduled test, is followed by a post-incident review documenting what worked, what did not, and any gaps between the plan and what the response actually required. Findings are tracked to closure and reviewed by the Change Advisory Board.

Independent of any real event, every Tier 1 system's recovery plan is tested at least once per calendar year through a scheduled failover exercise, and the results are logged in the same registry used for real DR events.
4.5 Plan Maintenance

A recovery plan that has not been reviewed since the system it describes was last significantly re-architected is not a plan the company can rely on. Every Tier 1 and Tier 2 system's recovery plan must be reviewed by its owning team whenever that system undergoes a material architecture change, and at minimum once per year even absent such a change, with the review date logged alongside the annual test date in the same registry.

Plans are written to be executable by whoever is on call, not only by the engineer who wrote them; a plan that only one specific person can follow is treated as a finding at the next annual test and is prioritized for rewriting in plain, step-by-step language.
4.6 Multi-Region and Multi-Provider Architecture

A Tier 1 system's recovery plan documents whether its failover target is a secondary region with the same cloud infrastructure provider, a standby environment with a different provider, or a degraded-mode configuration that serves reduced functionality from the primary region alone. Each option carries a different RTO in practice, and the plan is required to state the option actually tested most recently, not merely the option that is architecturally possible in principle.

Where a system's failover target depends on a Critical-tier infrastructure vendor under the Vendor and Third-Party Risk Management Policy (POL-008), §4, that dependency is documented explicitly in the recovery plan, since a regional outage that affects both the primary and the failover target at the same provider defeats the purpose of the failover entirely. Site Reliability Engineering reviews this cross-dependency at least once a year as part of the annual test cycle, independent of whether the underlying infrastructure vendor relationship itself is up for reassessment that year.
4.7 Communication and Status Page

The moment a DR event is declared, the Incident Commander designates a communications lead — typically the on-call Product Manager — who is responsible for updating the public status page and any proactive customer notifications on a fixed cadence, independent of the technical response. Status updates during a DR event follow the same cadence discipline as a Sev1 incident under the Incident Management and Response Policy (POL-005), §4: at minimum every thirty minutes while the event remains active, even if the update is only to say the situation is unchanged.

Internal communication runs on a separate channel from the customer-facing one, so that the technical detail engineers need to coordinate a failover — which is often more specific and more uncertain in the early minutes than anything appropriate to publish externally — never leaks into a customer-visible update before the Product Manager has had a chance to review it.
4.8 Tabletop Exercises versus Live Failover Tests

A tabletop exercise walks the owning team through the recovery plan verbally against a hypothetical scenario, without actually redirecting production traffic; it is faster to run and lower-risk, which is why it is the standard annual requirement for Tier 2 systems. A live failover test actually executes the documented steps against production or a production-equivalent environment and is the only kind of test that reliably surfaces a plan step that looks correct on paper but fails in practice — a runbook command that has quietly stopped working, a credential that expired, or a dependency that was never accounted for.

Because a live test carries real risk to the system under test, it is scheduled with the same change-management rigor as any other production change under the Software Change Management Policy (POL-001), §4, including a defined rollback point if the test itself needs to be aborted partway through. A live test that has to be aborted is still logged as a completed test for that year, with the abort itself treated as a finding to be addressed before the next attempt, rather than as a reason to skip testing that system for another cycle.
4.9 Backup Integrity and Restore Verification

A backup that has never been restored is not a verified recovery capability, only an assumption of one. Every Tier 1 system's owning team performs a documented restore-and-verify exercise — restoring from an actual backup into an isolated environment and confirming data integrity — at least quarterly, independent of and in addition to the annual full failover test, which exercises the broader coordination and traffic-redirection steps rather than backup integrity specifically.

A failed restore-and-verify exercise is treated as a Sev2-equivalent finding under the Incident Management and Response Policy (POL-005), §4, escalated immediately rather than queued for the next scheduled review, since a broken backup discovered only during a real disruption is one of the most severe failure modes this policy exists to prevent. The finding is not considered closed until a subsequent restore-and-verify exercise against the same system succeeds.
4.10 Cross-Functional Dependencies and Third-Party Coordination

Few Tier 1 systems recover in isolation: a customer-facing application typically depends on a database, a message queue, an identity provider, and often a Critical-tier external vendor under the Vendor and Third-Party Risk Management Policy (POL-008), §4. A system's recovery plan documents each of these dependencies explicitly and states what happens to the dependent system if each one is unavailable, rather than assuming every dependency will simply recover in lockstep with the system that relies on it.

Where a dependency is itself owned by another internal team, that team's on-call is included in the affected system's annual test, not merely notified after the fact; a recovery plan that has never actually coordinated with its own upstream or downstream teams during a test is considered unverified for that dependency, even if the system's own steps have been tested in isolation.

Coordination with an external Critical-tier vendor during an annual test is typically a scheduling and communication exercise rather than a technical one, since most vendor contracts do not grant the company the ability to trigger a test failover on the vendor's own infrastructure. In that case, the recovery plan instead documents the vendor's published RTO/RPO commitments and the company's own contingency if the vendor's actual recovery falls short of what was documented, which is reviewed for currency at each annual test cycle even though no live technical test against the vendor's systems is performed.
4.11 Extended and Cascading Disruptions

Most DR events resolve within the standard RTO windows in Table 2, but the response escalates further if recovery is still incomplete after twice the system's documented RTO has elapsed, or if the disruption spreads to affect a second Tier 1 system that was not part of the original declaration. At that point the Incident Commander convenes a standing bridge with the affected systems' Engineering Managers and the Product Manager to reassess the recovery approach rather than continuing to execute a plan that the evidence suggests is not working as documented.

An extended disruption crossing this threshold is automatically escalated to the executive team regardless of customer-facing severity, since a recovery that is taking meaningfully longer than planned is itself informative about the plan's quality and may require executive-level decisions — additional budget for emergency infrastructure, a public communication beyond the standard status page update, or accepting a degraded-mode configuration for longer than originally intended.
4.12 Annual DR Readiness Report

Following the last scheduled test of the calendar year, the Site Reliability Engineer who owns this policy compiles an annual DR readiness report covering every Tier 1 and Tier 2 system: whether its required test was completed, the RTO/RPO actually achieved against the target, and any open findings from either a real DR event or a test. This report is reviewed by the Change Advisory Board and forms part of the evidence presented at the company's annual ISO/IEC 27001 surveillance audit.

A system that has not completed its required annual test by the report's compilation date is listed as non-compliant rather than omitted from the report, and its owning Engineering Manager is required to present a remediation timeline to the Change Advisory Board at the same session. This report is the single artifact leadership relies on to know, at a glance, how much of the company's actual recovery capability has been verified this year versus how much remains an untested assumption.
5. References
Incident Management and Response Policy (POL-005), §4 — the standard incident escalation path that determines when a disruption is escalated toward formal DR activation.

Vendor and Third-Party Risk Management Policy (POL-008), §4 — governs vendor incident notification, which can itself trigger this policy's response when a Critical-tier vendor supports a Tier 1 system.

Software Change Management Policy (POL-001), §4 — governs how a live failover test itself is scheduled and, more generally, how any change made during recovery (including an emergency change) is logged and later reviewed.

External standards: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 (https://www.iso.org/standard/27001), business continuity management controls; ITIL 4 (https://www.axelos.com/certifications/itil-service-management), whose service continuity management practice this policy's five-stage lifecycle is modeled on.

The service criticality register and the per-system recovery plan templates referenced throughout this policy are maintained by Site Reliability Engineering and are available on the internal policy portal; this document defines the process, roles, and testing cadence, not the specific technical content of any one system's recovery plan.

Vendor and Third-Party Risk Management Policy (POL-008), §4 — governs the risk tiering, notification obligations, and reassessment cadence of any external vendor whose own incident could trigger this policy's response, and is the source of the vendor-dependency documentation referenced in §4.10.

Access Control and Least Privilege Policy (POL-006), §4 — governs break-glass and emergency access provisioned to responders during an active DR event, ensuring that elevated access granted under time pressure is still logged and time-boxed rather than left standing once the event concludes.
